gloss_terse: To turn, face, or direct oneself; clear a way; decline or pass away; by extension, to look toward or regard
gloss_readable: A verb of motion and orientation at its core, panah describes the physical act of turning one's body or redirecting one's course. In its various stems it extends from simple turning (Qal) to clearing or preparing a path (Piel), to causing something to turn (Hifil). The word also marks the passage of time ('at the turning of evening') and, more poignantly, the turning of God's attention toward a person in need. Arabic altafata and Korean dolaboda consistently render the physical act, while Spanish 'preparad' and Hebrew idiom reveal the Piel's distinctive sense of making ready.

senses.1: The dominant Qal sense of physically turning one's body or changing direction, attested 85 times. Arabic altafata (turn around) appears consistently, Korean dolaboda/dorikida (turned/turned back) confirms the kinetic core, and Swahili -geuka (turn) aligns. Exodus 2:12 shows Moses turning this way and that before striking the Egyptian; Exodus 32:15 has Moses turning and descending from the mountain.
senses.2: Static spatial orientation rather than active motion: something faces a direction without moving. Arabic muttajiha (directed/facing) and Korean hyanghanun (facing toward) distinguish this from active turning. Prominent in architectural descriptions such as 1 Kings 7:25, where the twelve oxen of the bronze sea face the four cardinal directions, and in boundary descriptions in Joshua 15.
senses.3: The Hifil causative: causing someone or something to turn. Arabic adaruu (they rotated something) and Korean dollyeoda (caused to turn) capture the causative agency. In Judges 15:4 Samson turns foxes tail to tail; in Jeremiah 46:5 warriors are turned back in flight. Only 8 occurrences, but the stem distinction is lexically significant.
senses.4: The Piel intensive-causative meaning to clear, prepare, or make ready a space or roadway. Arabic hayyiuu (prepare!) and ifsahuu (make room!) together with Korean yebihara (prepare!) confirm this as genuine preparation rather than mere turning. Isaiah 40:3 ('prepare the way of the LORD') and Psalm 80:9 ('you cleared ground before it') are the landmark passages.
senses.5: A temporal idiom built on the Qal infinitive construct with a preposition: 'at the turning of' evening or morning. Arabic inda iqbali (at the approach of) and Spanish 'al amanecer' (at dawn) show the metaphorical transfer from spatial turning to temporal transition. Genesis 24:63 ('at the turning of evening') and Exodus 14:27 ('at the turning of the morning') are the classic examples.
senses.6: An extension from physical turning to cognitive attention: looking at or regarding someone. Hindi dekha (saw) and Swahili -angalia (look at) confirm the perceptual shift. In Psalm 102:17 God 'turns toward' the prayer of the destitute, and in Haggai 1:9 the expected much 'turned to' little. Only 3 occurrences mark this as a contextual specialization.
senses.7: Temporal and figurative decline or passing away, as in Psalm 90:9 ('our years turn away like a sigh') and Jeremiah 6:4 ('the day declines'). Arabic fanat (perished) and mala (inclined/declined) use different roots from the core altafata, confirming genuine polysemy rather than vagueness. Spanish 'declina/declinaron' likewise marks the semantic shift.
senses.8: A single occurrence at Zephaniah 3:15 where the sense is turning away or removing, applied to God having turned away the judgments against Jerusalem. Spanish 'ha apartado' (has removed) and English 'he has turned away' suggest a removal-of-threat nuance distinct from mere physical turning.
senses.9: An isolated occurrence at Leviticus 14:36 in the context of the priestly law of leprosy in a house, where the command is to empty or evacuate the house before inspection. English 'and they shall empty' and Spanish 'y vaciarán' confirm this as a distinct action of clearing out contents, related to the Piel 'clearing' sense but applied to objects rather than a path.
senses.10: A single substantival or participial use at 2 Chronicles 25:23 where panah functions as part of a compound designation for a corner or corner-point of the wall. English 'the corner' and Spanish 'la Esquina' render this as a structural feature, deriving from the notion of a turning point in a wall's course.

gloss_terse: To afflict, humble, oppress; reflexively to fast or practice self-denial; to violate sexually
gloss_readable: One of the Hebrew Bible's most theologically weighted verbs, anah II spans a range from physical oppression to spiritual discipline. In its Piel stem it describes taskmasters afflicting Israel in Egypt (Exod 1:11) and the divine command to 'afflict your souls' on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:29). The Hitpael reflexive captures the act of voluntary fasting and humbling oneself before God (Ezra 8:21). A darker specialized sense covers sexual violation (Gen 34:2, 2 Sam 13:14). Arabic dhallala (humiliate) and qahara (oppress), Korean gotonghada (suffer) and geumsikhada (fast), and Swahili -tesa (afflict) together map the wide semantic territory.

senses.1: The primary Piel transitive sense of actively causing suffering, distress, or oppression. Arabic qahara (oppress) and adhalla (humiliate) capture the range, while Korean goerophida (cause distress) and Swahili -tesa (torment) confirm the cross-linguistic pattern. Genesis 15:13 foretells that Abraham's descendants will be afflicted four hundred years; Exodus 1:11-12 narrates the Egyptian taskmasters' oppression of Israel.
senses.2: Piel humbling that emphasizes reduction of status or pride rather than physical pain. Korean gyeomsonhage hada (make humble) and Arabic adhabahu (discipline him) capture the pedagogical nuance. Deuteronomy 8:2-3 is the key passage: God humbled Israel in the wilderness, feeding them with manna to teach dependence. The emphasis falls on internal transformation rather than external suffering.
senses.3: The Hitpael reflexive: to humble oneself or afflict one's soul, closely associated with fasting and penitential self-denial. Korean geumsikhada (fast) and Swahili kujinyenyekeza (humble oneself) reveal the ritual dimension. Leviticus 16:29-31 prescribes this for the Day of Atonement; Ezra 8:21 records a communal fast to seek God's protection for the journey to Jerusalem.
senses.4: The intransitive Qal expressing a state of being afflicted or bowed down without specifying an external agent. Spanish 'fui afligido' (I was afflicted) and French 'afflige' render the experiential standpoint. Psalm 119:67 ('before I was afflicted I went astray') and Psalm 116:10 use this to voice the psalmist's own suffering as formative spiritual experience.
senses.5: The Nifal reflexive-passive of being humbled or brought into submission, often with a posture of meekness or acceptance. Isaiah 53:7 is the paradigmatic text: 'he was oppressed and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth.' Arabic khadaa (submitted) and Swahili -nyenyekea (be humble) confirm the tone of yielded endurance.
senses.6: A specialized Piel usage denoting sexual violation or rape. Korean gangganghada (violate sexually) and Arabic ightasabaha (ravished her) sharply distinguish this from general affliction. Genesis 34:2 (Shechem and Dinah), 2 Samuel 13:14 (Amnon and Tamar), and the Deuteronomic laws of chapter 22 are the defining contexts.
senses.7: The Pual passive of the Piel: being subjected to affliction or oppression by an external agent. Spanish 'y afligido' (and afflicted) and German 'betruebte' (grieved) render the passive dimension. Isaiah 53:4 ('he has borne our griefs') and Psalm 132:1 ('remember David and all his afflictions') exemplify this form.
senses.8: Three occurrences where the gloss data reflects 'answer/respond,' likely stemming from the homonymous root anah I (H6030) rather than anah II. English 'and Your humility' (2 Sam 22:36) and Spanish 'les respondera' (Joel 2:19) show the overlap. These may represent tagging ambiguity in the source data, but the passages themselves blend the roots' meanings in illuminating ways.
senses.9: The Hifil causative: to cause affliction or bring someone into a state of oppression. A rarer stem variant that overlaps with the Piel but foregrounds the causal agent's initiative. Attested at 1 Kings 8:35 and 2 Chronicles 6:26 in Solomon's temple dedication prayer, both requesting God to hear when the people are afflicted.
senses.10: A single occurrence at Psalm 88:1 in the superscription 'le'annoth' (for afflicting or for singing), whose interpretation remains debated. Spanish 'para afligir' and French 'a humilier' take the affliction reading. Some scholars connect it instead to anah III (sing), making it a musical direction. The ambiguity itself witnesses to the lexical density of this root.

gloss_terse: To be sick, weak, or wounded; to grieve; causatively to make ill; reflexively to feign sickness
gloss_readable: Halah is the Hebrew Bible's primary vocabulary of illness, weakness, and physical vulnerability. In its Qal stem it describes kings falling sick (1 Kings 14:1, 2 Kings 20:1), Samson becoming weak (Judg 16:7), and the psalmist's grief (Ps 77:10). The Hifil causative extends the range to inflicting sickness (Isa 53:10, 'the LORD was pleased to crush him, making him sick'), while the Hitpael reflexive captures the memorable ruse of Amnon feigning illness to lure Tamar (2 Sam 13:2-6). Arabic marida (be sick) and Korean apuda (be in pain/ill) consistently track the core meaning across languages.

senses.1: The basic Qal sense of being in a state of physical sickness, the most frequent use at 27 occurrences. Arabic marida (be sick) and Korean byeongi deulda (fall ill) are consistent renderings. Genesis 48:1 ('your father is sick') and 2 Kings 20:1 ('Hezekiah was sick unto death') are landmark passages. Swahili -ugua (be sick) and Spanish 'enfermo' confirm the cross-linguistic stability of this core sense.
senses.2: Physical weakness or feebleness distinguished from specific illness. Arabic daaufa (become weak) replaces marida in these contexts. The Samson narratives in Judges 16:7, 11, 17 are the defining occurrences: 'I will become weak and be like any other man.' Isaiah 14:10 and 57:10 extend this to exhaustion of resources or will.
senses.3: The Nifal participle describing a wound, plague, or blow as grievous or incurable. Arabic shadida (severe) and Korean gochil su eomneun (incurable) appear in renderings. Jeremiah 10:19 ('my wound is grievous'), Jeremiah 30:12 ('your hurt is incurable'), and Nahum 3:19 ('there is no healing for your wound') are characteristic. The domain assignment to economics likely reflects metaphorical use of 'inheritance' language in some contexts.
senses.4: The Hifil and Piel causative: making someone sick or inflicting illness. Korean apuge hada (cause to be in pain) and Arabic amradahu (made him sick) confirm the causative agency. Isaiah 53:10 is theologically paramount: 'the LORD was pleased to crush him, making him sick.' Micah 6:13 threatens divine sickness as judgment; Proverbs 13:12 says 'hope deferred makes the heart sick.'
senses.5: The Qal participle feminine used attributively to describe an experience or situation as grievous or distressing. Ecclesiastes 5:13 and 5:16 call hoarding wealth a 'grievous evil,' employing the same root that elsewhere denotes bodily sickness. Jeremiah 4:31 uses the feminine participle in a simile of a woman in labor. The metaphorical extension from physical to existential malaise is clear.
senses.6: The Hofal passive: being severely wounded, particularly in battle. Korean jungseungeul ipda (receive a serious wound) and Spanish 'estoy herido' (I am wounded) render the passive military sense. 1 Kings 22:34 and 2 Chronicles 18:33 narrate Ahab's mortal wounding at Ramoth-gilead; 2 Chronicles 35:23 records Josiah's fatal wound at Megiddo.
senses.7: The Nifal expressing a state of weakness or infirmity, used substantively. Ezekiel 34:4 and 34:21 indict Israel's shepherds for failing to strengthen 'the weak' (hannehalot). Daniel 8:27 records Daniel himself falling ill after his vision. Arabic daaif (weak/infirm) and Swahili dhaifu (feeble) capture the substantival quality.
senses.8: The Hitpael reflexive: feigning or pretending to be sick. All three occurrences cluster in the narrative of Amnon's plot against Tamar (2 Sam 13:2, 5, 6). Korean apeun chekhada (pretend to be sick) and Spanish 'hazte enfermo' (make yourself sick) confirm the reflexive-pretense reading. This is a vivid example of the Hitpael stem's capacity for simulated action.
senses.9: Emotional or psychological suffering, grief, or hurt extending beyond physical illness. Psalm 77:10 ('this is my grief') and Proverbs 23:35 ('they struck me but I was not hurt') use halah for inner anguish. 1 Samuel 22:8 voices Saul's complaint that no one 'is sick' on his behalf, meaning no one grieves for him. Arabic hazina (grieve) and Korean seulpeohada (be sorrowful) mark the emotional register.
senses.10: The Nifal sense of becoming exhausted or worn out through sustained effort or futile labor. Jeremiah 12:13 declares 'they have worn themselves out but profit nothing,' and Amos 6:6 notes those at ease who 'are not grieved' over the ruin of Joseph. Arabic ajhada nafsahu (exhausted himself) and Korean jichida (be exhausted) confirm the semantic extension from sickness to depletion.

gloss_terse: Upon, on, over; against; beside; because of; concerning; for, on behalf of; to, unto; according to
gloss_readable: The preposition al is one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible, occurring nearly 5,800 times with a remarkable breadth of relational meanings radiating from its core spatial sense of 'upon' or 'on top of.' From physical surface contact it extends to adversative ('against'), proximity ('beside, at'), causal ('because of'), topical ('concerning'), benefactive ('on behalf of'), directional ('unto'), and normative ('according to') uses. Arabic ala provides a near-perfect cognate, while the diversity of renderings across target languages -- Korean wie-e (upon), daehangha-yeo (against), e daehayeo (concerning), and Swahili juu ya (on top), dhidi ya (against), kuhusu (about) -- reveals how one Hebrew preposition maps to many distinct relational concepts.

senses.1: The overwhelmingly dominant spatial sense (5,443 of 5,769 occurrences): surface contact, superposition, or vertical superiority. Arabic ala (upon), Korean wie (on/above), and Swahili juu ya (on top of) are uniform. Genesis 22:9 ('laid him on the altar') and Exodus 25:22 ('from above the mercy seat') illustrate the vertical range from contact to hovering presence.
senses.2: The adversative sense of opposition or hostility, attested 120 times. Arabic ala shifts to a hostile register, Korean daehangha-yeo (opposing) and daejeokha-yeo (resisting) replace the spatial wie, and Swahili dhidi ya (against) distinctly replaces juu ya. Genesis 50:20 ('you meant it against me') and Deuteronomy 15:9 ('a cry against you') are key passages showing the metaphorical leap from 'upon' to 'against.'
senses.3: Proximity or locative adjacency: being beside, by, or at a location without necessarily being on top of it. Arabic inda (at/beside) replaces ala in these contexts, and Korean eseo (at) and yeope (beside) appear alongside Swahili karibu na (near) and kando ya (alongside). Genesis 24:13 ('I am standing by the spring of water') and 24:43 ('beside the spring') exemplify this spatial softening.
senses.4: Causal and inferential use: 'because of,' 'on account of,' 'therefore.' Arabic min ajli (because of) and bisababi (on account of), Korean geureumeuro (therefore) and ttaemune (because of), and Swahili kwa sababu ya (because of) all mark the causal shift. Numbers 18:24 and 21:14 show al introducing the ground or reason for a preceding statement.
senses.5: Topical or referential use indicating 'concerning' or 'about' a subject matter. Arabic an (about) accompanies ala, Korean e daehayeo (regarding), and Swahili kuhusu (about/concerning) confirm the shift from spatial to discursive reference. Genesis 21:11 ('the matter was very grievous concerning his son') and 41:15 ('I have heard it said about you') are illustrative passages.
senses.6: Benefactive or purpose sense: 'for,' 'on behalf of,' 'for the sake of.' Arabic min ajlika/liajli (for the sake of), Korean reul wihayeo (for/on behalf of), and Swahili kwa ajili ya (for the sake of) converge. Leviticus 16:30 ('on this day atonement shall be made for you') and Leviticus 8:34 ('to make atonement on your behalf') are the defining sacral contexts.
senses.7: Directional or allative sense indicating motion toward: 'to,' 'unto.' Arabic ila (to/toward) replaces ala in these contexts, Korean ege (to someone), and Swahili hadi (up to) and kwake (to him) confirm genuine directional force. Exodus 3:18 and 5:3 ('let us go unto the LORD') and 2 Samuel 17:11 illustrate movement toward a goal or person.
senses.8: Normative and additive sense: 'according to' a standard or 'in addition to' something already mentioned. Arabic bihasabi (according to), Korean e ttara (in accordance with), and Swahili kulingana na (according to) and pamoja na (in addition to) map both sub-senses. Exodus 6:26 ('according to their hosts') and Numbers 1:18 ('according to their families') are typical of census and legal formulae.
senses.9: A cluster of 7 occurrences where al combines with min to form me'al (from upon), expressing removal or separation from a position on or over something. English 'from upon us,' Spanish 'de sobre nosotros,' and German 'von auf uns' all preserve the compound preposition. Numbers 21:7 ('pray that he take the serpents from upon us') and 1 Samuel 6:20 ('who is able to stand before this holy God -- who will he go up from upon us?') show the separative nuance.
